text.p: Swiss cargo surveyor group Societe Generale de Surveillance (SGS) Holding SA announced a 14 percent rise in 1996 net profits on Monday but said uncertainty over big Indonesia and Pakistan contracts may hit 1997 revenues.

The world leader in inspection and testing of cargoes said profit after tax, minority interests and goodwill amortisation rose to 262.7 million Swiss francs from 230.4 million in 1995 while consolidated revenues rose 12.4 percent to 2.95 billion.

SGS President Elizabeth Salina Amorini, whose family owns majority of the Geneva-based firm, said the group would propose a dividend rise to 13.20 francs per share from 11.20 for registered shares and to 66.00 from 56.00 for bearer shares.
With a global network of 37,000 staff, SGS inspects and monitors exports and imports of agricultural and mineral products, petroleum, petrochemicals, industrial equipment and consumer goods.

Founded in 1878, the company tries to minimise client risks by providing independent assessment and advice on services from monitoring coal cargoes in Australia to checking oil pipelines in Siberia and testing coffee exports from Rwanda and Uganda.

The SGS said a stronger dollar, the dominant currency in its business, would be positive for 1997 but that results could suffer if it failed to save lucrative preshipment inspection (PSI) contracts with the governments of Pakistan and Indonesia.

Indonesia, the SGS's biggest government client, terminated a PSI contract from March 31 ahead of the resumption of import inspection by its customs service. Pakistan too unexpectedly ended its PSI programme with SGS effective from March 12, 1997.
"Earnings would go down if we can't save these contracts. Indonesia is our biggest government contract," said Paul Lilley, SGS's chief financial officer.
SGS's 35 governmental contracts contributed to 25-26 percent of its global turnover in 1996. Amorini and Lilly declined to give the share of Indonesia and Pakistan.

The SGS said revenues from inspection and testing services, representing 75.5 percent of the group's total revenues, rose 11 percent in 1996 to 2.23 billion Swiss francs while revenues from agricultural services grew by 11.6 percent to 363 million.

Revenues from mineral services rose 8.6 percent to 352 million Swiss francs, from petroleum and petrochemical services rose nine percent to 315 million francs and from industry and consumer goods services rose 14.1 percent to 999 million francs.
Total revenues from services to the insurance industry rose 15.7 percent to 550.4 million Swiss francs.
SGS subsidiary GAB which handles claim valuations for insurance companies had been in the red until recently but made a modest profit in 1996 following a restructuring, Amorini said.
The company announced the following results (million Sfr unless stated)
Group net 262.7 vs 230.4
Pre-tax profit 361.5 vs 299.5
Net per regd share 30.50 vs 25.87
Net per bearer 152.65 vs 129.33
Operating profit 317.4 vs 250.0
Operating margin 10.7 pct vs 9.5 pct
Goodwill amortisation 1.8 vs 0.2
Cash flow 394.3 vs 341.3
Exceptional income 23.8 vs 1.5 (loss)
Net financial revenues 44.1 vs 49.5
Revenues 2,953.5 vs 2,627.9
-- Elif Kaban, Reuters Geneva Newsroom 41-22-733 38 31
